title: Forests identify built-environment associations in recorded drug-crime patterns
summary: Random forests analyzed 52,567 reported drug-related incidents in Chicago during 2016–2019. Vacant lots and buildings ranked highly in models distinguishing recorded heroin and synthetic-drug clusters. These are neighborhood-level associations in police records, not causal effects or measures of individuals’ behavior.
ai_technology: Space-time random forest; guided regularized random forest; partial dependence
organization: University of Maryland; Oak Ridge National Laboratory

evidence.tested: Forest feature selection and importance analysis compared recorded cluster patterns with built-environment, demographic and lagged variables.
evidence.unknown: Policing practices were unavailable and may influence recorded patterns; ecological associations do not identify individual risk or prove neighborhood causes. Temporal-window selection used the studied series. No treatment-service or policing benefit was tested.
evidence.ai_role: Forest ensembles learn nonlinear feature combinations; corrected importance and partial dependence characterize the source-specific observed spatial associations.

source_review.scope: Indexed primary data/model/feature-selection Methods, Results and limitations; exact primary front date/affiliations and fresh primary notice metadata.
